idiom_name: BTreeMap window (first_key_value / pop_first) + Mutex or Tokio channel
implementation_notes: Rust's standard library has an ideal ordered window - BTreeMap iterates in key order and first_key_value/pop_first expose the head - but no resequencer, so the cursor, the capacity bound and the gap policy are hand-written. In synchronous code a Mutex<BTreeMap<u64, Msg>> plus Receiver::recv_timeout covers window and deadline; in async code one task owns the map and selects over the inbound channel and tokio::time::sleep, which is the same structure without holding a lock across await. When the disorder comes from concurrently polled futures rather than from the transport, futures::stream::FuturesOrdered already yields results in the order the futures were inserted.
pitfalls: BTreeMap::remove needs the exact key, so after a gap deadline the cursor must be moved to the new head explicitly; otherwise the window waits forever on a key that never arrives.
Holding a std::sync::MutexGuard across an .await does not compile and is not Send; an async resequencer should own the map in one task instead of locking it.
Windows must be bounded: an unbounded BTreeMap is a memory denial-of-service, so evict by capacity and decide whether an evicted message is dropped or the whole correlation is failed.
